title: Quanta Services Raises Guidance as Big Tech Capex Pressures Grid Capacity
subtitle: While hyperscalers burn billions on computing power, the contractor stringing the high-voltage lines is printing record cash.
summary: Quanta lifted full-year guidance across the board after posting record quarterly free cash flow and a $63.7 billion backlog. The performance highlights how physical grid construction is separating itself from the financial strain hitting Big Tech balance sheets.

bodyHtml:
The market spent late October punishing anything tied to the artificial intelligence buildout. Tech investors suddenly recoiled at the sheer cost of running the trade, pushing the Nasdaq down nearly 3 percent on Friday. Alphabet posted negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion. Amazon burned $42.4 billion on a trailing basis. The four largest hyperscalers and SpaceX are on pace to spend $828 billion on capital expenditures this year. Yet while Silicon Valley bleeds cash on computing infrastructure, the contractor physically wiring those servers had a very different story to tell. Quanta Services is North America's biggest electrical-infrastructure contractor. In plain English, they do the heavy lifting the modern economy cannot survive without. Quanta employs roughly 95,000 workers, mostly linemen, welders and equipment operators, to build high-voltage transmission lines, substations and underground conduits. If hyperscalers are building digital skyscrapers, Quanta is the plumber laying the high-voltage pipes that turn the power on. The electric segment produces roughly 82 percent of revenue, but tech giants racing to build computing campuses now crowd its client list.

That makes Quanta the gatekeeper of the AI era. The International Energy Agency expects data center power consumption to reach 945 terawatt-hours by 2030, with the US consuming nearly half of that total. But servers cannot run on good intentions. Lawrence Berkeley National Lab counts over 2,000 gigawatts of generation and storage trapped in interconnection queues across roughly 8,200 projects, with median wait times exceeding five years. Regional grid operator PJM now forecasts summer peak electricity demand growing 3.6 percent annually through 2036, up from 0.3 percent a few years ago. Interconnection is the single biggest bottleneck in computing, and Quanta gets paid to shorten the wait. The company's third-quarter report showed what happens when that bottleneck meets contracted work. Revenue jumped 57 percent to $12.01 billion, and stripping out acquisitions it still grew 37 percent. Adjusted EBITDA rose 69 percent to $1.45 billion, while quarterly free cash flow hit a record $1.2 billion. Quanta raised full-year guidance across every single operating metric and prepaid a $619 million term loan. As chief executive Duke Austin told analysts: "The five largest technology companies will spend three times the capital budget of the utility side. We can perform vast majority of that capital other than chips." Quanta's competitive moat is physical bodies and scarce equipment. Austin put it plainly on the call: "You cannot buy craft, you have to build it." Quanta added 26,000 workers this year, and about 12,000 of them came organically. Apprentices get trained from scratch, which drags on margins before it pays off. To sidestep equipment shortages, the firm is standing up manufacturing in 10 states for the long-lead gear its crews need, building its own transformers, breakers and poles. Controlling that supply chain keeps its people in the field while rival projects wait months for switchgear. For the equity, the re-rating story hinges on backlog quality. Quanta already commands a premium because it rides two separate cycles: utility modernization and tech capex. What pushes the valuation higher from here is not revenue growth, but whether multi-year technology bids convert into firm, high-margin commitments. Firm contractual obligations doubled year-over-year to nearly $42 billion. Management insists visibility now stretches past 2030, but the market will reward the stock only if large-load data projects drive double-digit earnings growth into 2027. The bear case argues that investors are paying premium multiples for cyclical construction risk. Growth looks flattering because Quanta spent over $1.2 billion upfront on four acquisitions, generating a $1.51 per share gap between GAAP and adjusted earnings through intangible amortization. More importantly, roughly $22 billion of its $63.7 billion total backlog consists of estimated master service agreements rather than binding orders. Adding tens of thousands of workers also creates training overhead before productivity ramps up. If hyperscalers slash their budgets, complex large-load projects like Quanta's three-gigawatt buildout with NiSource are precisely the initiatives developers delay first. We are watching whether Quanta's twelve-month backlog can keep expanding sequentially when fourth-quarter numbers drop early next year. As long as cloud giants need electricity faster than utilities can supply it, the linemen stringing the wire hold all the leverage.
